summary: Lists requirements for Advanced Multipath in MPLS networks. Advanced Multipath formalizes multipath techniques already used in IP and MPLS networks, such as link bundling and composite links, and adds extensions to them.

eli5.summary: When one road is too small, you can use several roads at once and split the cars among them. This document lists what we need so that works well for the internet's label-switched traffic.

subtitle: Requirements for splitting MPLS traffic across parallel links

tldr.problem: Core networks need to send huge amounts of traffic that exceed the capacity of a single link or router. When parallel links exist with different characteristics like latency, network operators need formal requirements for how to distribute traffic across them.
tldr.mechanism: Advanced Multipath formalizes multipath techniques already in use (link bundling, ECMP) and adds extensions for links with different characteristics, while maintaining packet ordering, stability, and performance objectives.
tldr.outcome: This document provides functional, protocol, and management requirements that solutions must meet, supporting diverse link characteristics while ensuring traffic flows do not reorder and performance objectives are met.

today: RFC 7226 is an Informational RFC defining requirements for Advanced Multipath in MPLS networks. It has not been obsoleted and remains the reference for multipath protocol and solution design.

sections.title: The Need for Multiple Paths
sections.content:
Core networks today face bandwidth demands that far exceed the capacity of a single physical link or processing element. Multipath—distributing traffic across multiple paths such that each packet stays on one path and is not reordered—is already used in networks through link bundling, Ethernet aggregation, and Equal Cost Multipath (ECMP) techniques.

The presence of parallel links, each potentially comprised of multiple layers, introduces new requirements. Some services may need to be restricted to specific links when characteristics like latency differ. Others require that a Label Switched Path (LSP) be atomic and avoid any reordering. Advanced Multipath is a formalization of these multipath techniques that meets the requirements in this document, with key support for non-homogeneous (different) component links.

This document enumerates requirements related to protocols and mechanisms that provide MPLS-based Advanced Multipath, organized into functional requirements (what the system must do), general protocol requirements (how protocols should work), and management requirements.
sections.eli5: Big networks need many roads to handle all the traffic. Different roads have different speed and reliability, so we need rules for how to pick which road each message takes.

sections.title: Key Concepts and Definitions
sections.content:
Multipath means traffic can take more than one path from one node to a destination, where each packet takes one path only (no subdivision or resequencing). Advanced Multipath Group (AMG) is a collection of component links where Advanced Multipath techniques apply. Component links are individual links in the multipath; they may be physical links or logical links that preserve packet ordering.

A composite link (formalized by ITU-T) combines multiple component links. The document explicitly excludes inverse multiplexing, which resequences packets at the receiving end—unsuitable for very high-bandwidth applications. Client LSP is an LSP set up over one or more lower layers, including over an AMG. A flow is a sequence of packets that should be transferred in order on one component link.

Load balance means subdividing traffic over component links such that load is fairly evenly distributed while meeting packet ordering requirements. Performance objective is a numerical value for performance measures (availability, latency, delay variation), related to Service Level Agreements or internal requirements.
sections.eli5: Component links are the individual roads. An AMG is the whole group of roads. A flow is traffic that needs to stay on one road. Load balance means spreading traffic fairly so no road gets overloaded.

sections.title: Functional Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC groups functional requirements by priority, starting with the most critical.

Availability and stability: Transient periods after failures must stay within performance objective time frames. An AMG should behave as a single IGP adjacency but may announce detailed parameters about component links. Convergence times and restoration operations must meet existing performance objectives. The solution must allow path selection such that flows within an LSP are distributed across paths while meeting other requirements.

Different link characteristics: Network operators deploy lower-layer networks with diversity—component links with different latencies or other characteristics. The solution must allow the client layer to indicate preferences for minimum-latency links, maximum-acceptable latency, and maximum delay variation. These requirements support quality-of-service for flows needing specific performance profiles.

Bidirectional LSPs: Some client LSPs require paths bound to specific component links; this is most common in bidirectional LSPs carrying timing protocols. Others only require the LSP serve the same set of nodes in both directions. The solution must allow binding to specific links and support co-routed bidirectional LSPs bound to the same node set.

Load balancing dynamics: Load balancing must avoid oscillation. The solution must distribute flows across component links to meet performance objectives, measure traffic flows and dynamically select component links to prevent overload, move flows minimally disruptively, and allow operators to control the frequency of link changes. Client LSPs can optionally refuse splitting across links.
sections.eli5: When something breaks, traffic should reroute quickly. Different roads can have different speed. If two directions need the same route, the system should support that. Traffic should be spread fairly and not jump around constantly.

sections.title: Protocol Solution Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC specifies how protocol solutions should be designed. Solutions should extend existing protocols (extending LDP where possible without defining LDP Traffic Engineering methods). Both LDP-signaled and RSVP-TE-signaled LSPs must coexist on an AMG, and management-plane setup must also be supported.

When nodes are in the same routing domain, extensions to Interior Gateway Protocols (IGP) are allowed. When nodes are in different MPLS network topologies, solutions must not rely on IGP extensions. AMG IGP advertisement should result in faster convergence than advertising individual component links and minimize advertisement-update frequency to avoid destabilizing the routing system.

In worst-case failure scenarios, the number of client LSPs requiring re-signaling must not cause a period of unavailability that significantly exceeds existing provider performance objectives. Processing load from IGP readvertisement and resignaling time must not increase significantly compared to current methods.
sections.eli5: New protocols should build on existing ones rather than replacing them. Routers should understand the group of roads as a single unit in their routing calculations. Recovery from failures should not take much longer than today.

sections.title: Management and Operational Considerations
sections.content:
The management plane must support polling the status and configuration of an AMG and its individual component links, and must notify on status change. Operators must be able to activate or deactivate any component link to facilitate maintenance; routers must redistribute traffic from deactivated links to others based on traffic engineering criteria.

The management plane must allow configuration of a client LSP over an AMG and selection of a component link, must trace which component link a client LSP uses and monitor performance, and must verify connectivity over each component link. Component link and AMG faults must notify the management plane; AMG faults must also be distributed via IGP link state messages.

Operators should be able to initiate optimization processes, which must happen in a minimally disruptive manner. A minimally disruptive change occurs with zero packet loss and may cause brief delay discontinuities (an isolated event greatly exceeding normal jitter), which is acceptable if rare. Delay discontinuities can cause reordering or gaps and may affect sensitive flows like timing distribution or circuit emulation.
sections.eli5: Network operators need tools to see what is happening, turn links on and off for maintenance, and optimize traffic without breaking active calls.

items.title: Component Link
items.text: Individual physical or logical link in the multipath.

items.title: Flow
items.text: Sequence of packets that stays on one component link.

items.title: Load Balance
items.text: Spreading traffic fairly across component links.

items.title: Performance Objective
items.text: Numerical targets for availability, latency, or delay.
